chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 221 to 230, Kapilar's kurinji decade in which every poem opens அம்ம வாழி தோழி: the heroine and her friend talk of the secret lover's comings and goings measured on her body, her brow paling and shoulders slackening when he speaks of leaving or stays away, and her golden beauty returning when he comes by night or comes at last for the wedding.

221.reading: The woman tells her friend that her lover says he will go back to his hill country, and at that word her chosen beauty, fine as a doll's, begins to fade and her lovely dark body to pale.
221.nuance: The harm is done by the announcement, not the journey: செல்வல் is a first-person future quoted, and the fading and paling are set against the saying itself.

thinai_evidence.note: his land is the land of hills; the parting is to his own country, not across the waste

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; என் ஆய்கவின் makes the heroine the speaker

222.reading: The woman asks her friend whether it is because the man of the fragrant cool chest, who used to come close and stay in their town, no longer comes as sweetly now, that her brow under its small rows of hair is turning pale.
222.nuance: She offers the cause as a question, as if the pallor were a riddle to be solved, though she names the answer herself; the question form lets her accuse him without saying it.

thinai_evidence.note: the secret lover's visits to her town falling off, a kalavu situation

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; என் நுதல் makes the heroine the speaker

223.reading: The woman tells her friend that on their hill, as water runs down the peaks and the glory lily grows tall, their lover has come back ahead of the cold dew season and its north wind that torment those parted from their lovers.
223.nuance: The season is named only to be beaten: the poem lists everything the cold time does to the parted, and the last line says he arrived before it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and the cold dew season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நம் காதலோர் could also be the friend's words to the heroine

224.reading: The woman tells her friend that bathing with them in the clear falls of their sapphire-dark hill was once easy for him, and that it should now have grown hard for him leaves her bewildered.
224.nuance: மன் marks the ease as something past and gone; the bewilderment is at the change in him, not at any obstacle she can see.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and its falls, the place of the lovers' play

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; மருண்டனென் யானே makes the heroine the speaker

225.reading: The woman asks her friend whether their lover does not perceive that the bright lovely brow of the soft one, whose hair is fragrant within with the cool blue lily that rises above the green leaves of the hill pool, is turning pale.
225.nuance: The heroine speaks of herself in the third person as மெல்லியல், setting her beauty out as if for him to see; the fragrance of the lily-filled hair is still there while the brow fails.

thinai_evidence.note: the blue lily of the hill pool

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; the soft one may be the heroine naming herself, or the friend may be speaking of her

226.reading: The friend tells the woman that the heartless man who took her strong, conquering beauty and then turned his back like the bee that drinks the pollen of the fragrant-clustered glory lily on the cool slope of their hill and leaves, has now come.
226.nuance: The bee simile fixes what kind of lover he was, one who took and went; his arrival is reported without forgiveness, so the friend's news is also a charge. Because the tenor is stated, the bee is a simile, not ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: the glory lily of the hill slope

comparisons.tenor: the man who enjoyed her beauty and turned away

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நின் கவின் makes the heroine the one addressed

227.reading: The woman asks her friend whether she has let go the oath he swore, since the man who won their trust by saying he could not bear to see her brow pale and her shoulders slacken day by day now lives apart from them.
227.nuance: The oath was sworn to the friend as witness, so only the friend could release it; the question turns his absence into the friend's doing, which is reproach and irony at once.

thinai_evidence.note: no native thing; the kalavu oath and the decade's place in the kurinji hundred decide

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நீ விட்டனையோ is put to the friend who witnessed the oath

228.reading: The woman asks her friend what will become of their dear life if the lord of the long hill with its falls spreading and shining goes away without pleading for their favour.
228.nuance: இரந்து குறையுறல் is the lover's suit to the friend in kalavu; the heroine fears not his absence in general but his leaving with that suit refused or unspoken, so she presses the friend to receive it.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the long hill and its falls

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நம் இன்னுயிர் could also be the friend's words, fearing for the heroine

229.reading: The friend asks the woman whether the man without virtue, who stayed away many days while they wept, came to her in the night, since her brow has taken on a golden, conquering beauty.
229.nuance: The friend reads the brow as evidence: the pallor's lifting betrays a night visit the heroine has not told of, so the question teases and also lets her know the secret is seen.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's coming by night, the kurinji hour

comparisons.tenor: the restored beauty of her brow

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நின் நுதல் makes the heroine the one addressed

230.reading: The friend tells the woman that for the lord of the hill country, who joined them as a guard of the little millet and then made her soft shoulders slacken, her lovely brow pale and her golden, conquering beauty fade, their people are now preparing the good wedding.
230.nuance: The friend lists the harm he did at the very moment she announces the wedding, so the marriage is framed as the settling of a debt rather than as a gift.

thinai_evidence.note: the guarded millet field of the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain அம்ம வாழி தோழி and the poem's own pronouns; நின் மெல்தோள் makes the heroine the one addressed; the wedding ends the kalavu

links.note: Kural 1156 says that a man who can speak of leaving leaves no hope; Ainkurunuru 221 shows the heroine's beauty fading at the quoted word செல்வல், before any journey begins.
links.teaches: The couplet judges the announcement as a moral sign of hardness, while the poem shows it working on the body at once, so together they make the spoken intention, not the absence, the first wound of parting in Tamil love poetry.

links.note: In Ainkurunuru 224 the heroine says bathing in the falls with them has become hard for him; in Akananuru 38 the friend imagines him finding the pool clear because the girls no longer leap in and bathe there.
links.teaches: The same lost bathing in the hill pool is blamed on his growing distance by the heroine and traced by the friend to the girls' own absence, so the end of shared play reads as neglect from inside the house and as confinement from the friend's wider view.

links.note: Kural 1188 says people call her pale but no one says he left her; Ainkurunuru 225 asks whether the lover himself does not perceive the paling of her brow.
links.teaches: Held together they show the pallor seen by the whole town yet unread by the one man it concerns, so the symptom that exposes her to gossip fails at the only task she wants of it, reaching him.

links.note: Both heroines face a lover who swore assurances to the friend and stays apart while her beauty fades; Natrinai 358's heroine goes to pray that the oath's god not harm him, Ainkurunuru 227's asks the friend whether she has released him from it.
links.teaches: An oath sworn before the friend binds the lover through a god's punishment, so the heroine is caught between wanting it held and fearing what holding it would do to him, and the two poems show the two halves of that bind.

links.note: Kural 1155 asks the friend to prevent the departure of the man fit for her, since union is hard once he goes; Ainkurunuru 228 asks what becomes of their life if he leaves without having pleaded for favour.
links.teaches: The poem supplies the mechanism the couplet leaves out: in secret love the man's suit must pass through the friend, so the heroine's plea that the friend stop his leaving is a plea that she accept his pleading.

links.note: Kural 1265 says the pallor of her shoulders will leave once she has seen her husband her eyes' fill; in Ainkurunuru 229 the friend sees the brow's golden beauty returned and asks whether he came in the night.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the lover's presence the cure for pallor, and the poem turns that rule into a means of detection, so the cure that the heroine longs for is also what betrays her secret meeting to the friend.

links.note: In Natrinai 386 the friend recalls the hill-lord coming humbly with the word வதுவை so that the village shone; in Ainkurunuru 230 the friend announces the wedding for the hill-lord who once guarded millet with them and wasted the heroine's beauty.
links.teaches: Both friends mark the wedding as the end of kalavu, but one remembers the suitor's humility and the other his damage, so the go-between's announcement of marriage could be told as the lover's submission or as payment of what he owed.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the refrain and from the poems' own pronouns (என் for the heroine speaking, நின் for the friend speaking), and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
222 line 3 இன் இனி is divided in our text; read as இன்னினி (now) or இன் (sweetly) with இனி, the sense uncertain.
223 line 2 வரையாம் இழிய is unclear; read as வரை ஆம் இழிய (water running down the peaks), uncertain.
227 line 3 ஆற்றலம் யாம் is read as the lover's own words (we could not bear it), uncertain.
